approved: Australian Veterans’ Recognition (Putting Veterans and Their Families First) Bill 2019

The speaker introduced the Australian Veterans' Recognition (Putting Veterans and Their Families First) Bill 2019, which enshrines an Australian Defence Veterans' Covenant in legislation, provides a veterans card and lapel pin for anyone with a single day of service, and includes a statement supporting beneficial interpretation of veterans legislation.

The speaker supported the Australian Veterans' Recognition Bill 2019, which establishes the Australian Defence Veterans' Covenant, but argued it should be extended to include current serving personnel and their families, and include mandatory annual reporting to parliament. The speaker also supported amendments imposing a 90-day time limit for claims under the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Act, and criticised the government's rollout of the veterans card and discount scheme as botched and tokenistic.

The speaker supported the Australian Veterans' Recognition (Putting Veterans and Their Families First) Bill, noting Labor had announced plans for a defence personnel covenant in September last year and welcomed the government adopting that idea through the bill.

Labor supported the Australian Veterans' Recognition (Putting Veterans and Their Families First) Bill 2019, which establishes the Australian Defence Veterans' Covenant, despite concerns it excludes currently serving personnel and lacks annual reporting requirements. The member for Lyons noted that approximately 15,000 Tasmanians served in World War I and that fourteen Tasmanians have been awarded the Victoria Cross, including six from the Lyons electorate.

The member supported the Australian Veterans' Recognition Bill 2019 but questioned the practical benefits of lapel pins and veterans cards, noting that veterans in their electorate raised concerns about tokenism and instead advocated for fairer advocacy grant funding, improved DVA staff training, and resolution of DFRDB commutation issues. The bill enshrines the Australian Defence Force covenant in legislation and requires veterans' laws to be interpreted in their favour.

The bill establishes an Australian Defence Veterans' Covenant to enshrine the post-World War I social contract, with the speaker arguing it goes beyond symbolism to clarify government obligations; they noted 280,000 veterans and families are currently supported, about 5,500 personnel leave service each year, and called for greater flexibility in Department of Veterans' Affairs support.

The Labor MP supported the Australian Veterans' Recognition (Putting Veterans and Their Families First) Bill 2019, arguing it enshrines a national covenant recognising the unique nature of military service, but noted reservations that it does not cover currently serving members or include a legislated annual reporting requirement. The MP also called for a dedicated veterans' wellbeing centre in the Northern Territory.

The minister announced the Australian Defence Veterans' Covenant, a veterans card, and a veteran and reservist lapel pin as part of a recognition package, while expressing concerns about a Senate amendment requiring all claims under the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Act to be determined within 90 days. The government has committed nearly $500 million to transform the Department of Veterans' Affairs, with over 100,000 veterans using the MyService digital platform and 66,000 claims lodged.
